To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the vertical length of the food web is not a fixed value and that δ15N analysis can be used to estimate the vertical length of a food web.

(a) aquatic animals in real, global food webs are rarely observed above the fifth or six trophic categories and (b) the δ15N method is a useful tool for reconstructing trophic structure in aquatic systems, especially for food webs that have been altered by humans.

(i) the vertical length of aquatic food webs, as estimated by δ15N analysis, is similar to that of Elton’s “Pyramid of Numbers”, (ii) the vertical length is similar to that estimated from other recent compilations of δ15N data, and (iii) this length is shorter than that predicted by the Lindeman’s “Pyramid” of Energy”.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the application of stable isotope analysis to the study of food web structure and function.
the development of a mathematical model for describing the structure of a food web.
the application of stable isotope analyses of nitrogen (δ15N) to aquatic food webs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the “pyramid of biomass” is not a pyramid at all, but rather a “pyramid of mass” that is not constrained by the number of trophic levels, but by the number of organisms in the ecosystem.
aquatic food webs are generally 6–7 trophic levels in length and that they are not rigidly structured in a pyramid of energy.
the number of trophic categories in food webs is constrained by the number of trophi, but the vertical height of food webs is determined by the number of organisms in each trophic category.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
aquatic animals in food webs can rarely exceed a trophic level of 5 or 6.
the vertical length of aquatic food webs is about five or six trophic levels, but that the horizontal width of food webs may vary considerably depending on habitat and the presence of detritus.
aquatic food webs have a vertical dimension of 5–6 trophic categories.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the vertical length of aquatic food webs can be reliably predicted from the δ15N of the base trophic level (i.e. the primary producer) and the δ15N value of a consumer at the apex of the food web (i.e. a predator).
aquatic food webs are not as long and complex as previously thought.
aquatic food webs are not as rigidly structured as Lindeman’s energy pyramid would suggest, but they are not as flexible as some have claimed.
